paragraphs: “What do you think the doctor will say to him?” Kolya asked quickly. “What a repulsive face he has, though, don’t you think? I can’t stand medicine!”
“Ilusha is dying. I think that’s certain,” Alyosha answered sadly.
“They’re crooks! Medicine’s a fraud! I’m glad to have met you, though, Karamazov. I’ve wanted to know you for a long time. I’m only sorry we’re meeting in such sad circumstances.”
Kolya very much wanted to say something warmer and more heartfelt, but he felt awkward. Alyosha noticed this, smiled, and shook his hand.

“I learned long ago to respect you as a rare person,” Kolya muttered again, faltering and unsure. “I’ve heard you’re a mystic and that you were in the monastery. I know you’re a mystic, but ... that hasn’t put me off. Contact with real life will cure you.... It’s always like that with people like you.”
“What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?” Alyosha was rather astonished.
“Oh, God and all the rest of it.”
“What, you don’t believe in God?”

“Oh, I’ve nothing against God. Of course, God is only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He’s needed ... for the order of the universe and all that ... and that if there were no God, He would have to be invented,” added Kolya, beginning to blush. He suddenly thought Alyosha might take him to be showing off his knowledge and trying to prove he was “grown up.” “I haven’t the slightest wish to show off my knowledge to him,” Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt horribly annoyed.

“I have to say I can’t stand getting into such discussions,” he said, with an air of finality. “A person who doesn’t believe in God can love mankind, don’t you think? Voltaire didn’t believe in God, and he loved mankind, didn’t he?” (“I’m at it again,” he thought to himself.)

“Voltaire believed in God, though not very much, I think, and I don’t think he loved mankind very much either,” said Alyosha quietly, gently, and quite naturally, as though he were talking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck by how unsure Alyosha seemed of his own opinion of Voltaire. He seemed to be leaving the question for him, little Kolya, to settle.
“Have you read Voltaire?” Alyosha finished.
“No, not exactly read.... But I’ve read _Candide_ in the Russian translation ... in an absurd, grotesque, old translation ... (At it again! Again!)”
“And did you understand it?”

“Oh, yes, everything.... That is ... Why would you think I wouldn’t understand it? There’s a lot of nastiness in it, of course.... Of course I can see it’s a philosophical novel, written to argue for an idea....” Kolya was getting muddled by now. “I’m a Socialist, Karamazov, I’m an incurable Socialist,” he announced suddenly, out of nowhere.
“A Socialist?” Alyosha laughed. “But when did you find time to become one? Why, I thought you were only thirteen.”
Kolya winced.

“First of all, I’m not thirteen but fourteen, fourteen in two weeks,” he said, flushing angrily, “and second, I completely fail to see what my age has to do with it. The question is what my convictions are, not how old I am, isn’t it?”
“When you’re older, you’ll see for yourself how age affects convictions. I also thought you weren’t expressing your own ideas,” Alyosha answered calmly and modestly, but Kolya interrupted him hotly:

“Oh, come on, you want obedience and mysticism. You have to admit that the Christian religion, for instance, has only served the rich and the powerful, to keep the lower classes in slavery. That’s so, isn’t it?”
“Ah, I know where you read that, and I’m sure someone told you so!” cried Alyosha.

“Now, what makes you think I read it? And certainly no one told me so. I can think for myself.... I’m not against Christ, if you like. He was a most humane person, and if He were alive today, He’d be found in the ranks of the revolutionists, and might well play a prominent part.... There’s no doubt about that.”
“Oh, where, where did you get that from? What fool have you made friends with?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“Come on, the truth will out! It happens I’ve often talked to Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said that too, so they say.”
“Byelinsky? I don’t remember it. He didn’t write that anywhere.”
“If he didn’t write it, they say he said it. I heard that from a ... but never mind.”
“And have you read Byelinsky?”
“Well, no ... I haven’t read all of him, but ... I read the passage about Tatyana, about why she didn’t go off with Onyegin.”
“Why she didn’t go off with Onyegin? Surely you don’t ... understand that already?”

“Why, you seem to take me for little Smurov,” said Kolya, with a grin of irritation. “But please don’t think I’m such a revolutionist. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Though I mention Tatyana, I’m not at all for the emancipation of women. I accept that women are a subject race and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said.” Kolya, for some reason, smiled. “And on that question at least I’m completely of one mind with that pseudo-great man. I also think that leaving your own country and running off to America is contemptible, worse than contemptible—it’s silly. Why go to America when you can be of great service to humanity here? Especially now. There’s a whole mass of fruitful activity open to us. That’s what I answered.”
“What do you mean? Answered whom? Has someone already suggested you go to America?”

“I’ll admit they’ve been at me to go, but I refused. That’s between us, of course, Karamazov; do you hear, not a word to anyone. I’m telling this only to you. I’m not at all keen to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain bridge.
Long will you remember The house at the Chain bridge.

Do you remember? It’s splendid. Why are you laughing? You don’t think I’m lying, do you?” (“What if he finds out that I’ve only that one issue of _The Bell_ in father’s bookcase, and haven’t read any more of it?” Kolya thought with a shudder.)

“Oh, no, I’m not laughing, and don’t think for a moment that you’re lying. No, really, I can’t think so, because all this, alas, is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin—_Onyegin_, for instance?... You spoke just now of Tatyana.”
“No, I haven’t read it yet, but I want to. I have no prejudices, Karamazov; I want to hear both sides. Why do you ask?”
“Oh, nothing.”

“Tell me, Karamazov, do you have a terrible contempt for me?” Kolya rapped out suddenly and drew himself up in front of Alyosha, as though he were on drill. “Please tell me, and don’t beat about the bush.”
“Contempt for you?” Alyosha looked at him in wonder. “Why? I’m only sad that a charming nature like yours should be warped by all this crude nonsense before you’ve even begun life.”
“Don’t worry about my nature,” Kolya interrupted, not without complacency. “But it’s true that I’m stupidly sensitive, crudely sensitive. You smiled just now, and I thought you seemed to—”

“Oh, my smile meant something quite different. I’ll tell you why I smiled. Not long ago I read what a German who had lived in Russia wrote about our students and schoolboys today. ‘Show a Russian schoolboy,’ he writes, ‘a map of the stars, which he knows nothing about, and he will hand you back the map the next day with corrections on it.’ No knowledge and unbounded conceit—that’s what the German meant to say about the Russian schoolboy.”

“Yes, that’s perfectly right,” Kolya laughed suddenly, “exactly so! Bravo for the German! But he didn’t see the good side, don’t you think? Conceit, maybe, but that comes from youth, and it will be corrected if need be. On the other hand, there’s an independent spirit almost from childhood, a boldness of thought and conviction, and not the spirit of these sausage makers, groveling before authority.... But the German was right all the same. Bravo for the German! But Germans need strangling all the same. Though they’re so good at science and learning, they must be strangled.”
“Strangled, what for?” smiled Alyosha.

“Well, maybe I’m talking nonsense, I agree. I’m awfully childish sometimes, and when I’m pleased about something I can’t restrain myself and I’m ready to talk any rubbish. But, I say, we’re chattering away here about nothing, and that doctor has been in there a long time. But perhaps he’s examining the mamma and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. She whispered to me suddenly as I was leaving, ‘Why didn’t you come before?’ And in such a voice, so reproachfully! I think she’s awfully nice and pathetic.”

“Yes, yes! Well, you’ll be coming often, and you’ll see what she’s like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like that, to learn to value a great deal that you’ll find out from knowing these people,” Alyosha said warmly. “That would have more effect on you than anything.”
“Oh, how I regret it and blame myself for not coming sooner!” Kolya exclaimed, with bitter feeling.
“Yes, it’s a great pity. You saw for yourself how delighted the poor child was to see you. And how he fretted for you to come!”

“Don’t tell me! You make it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me from coming was my conceit, my egoistic vanity, and the beastly willfulness that I can never get rid of, though I’ve struggled with it all my life. I see that now. I’m a beast in lots of ways, Karamazov!”
“No, you have a charming nature, though it’s been distorted, and I quite understand why you’ve had such an influence on this generous, morbidly sensitive boy,” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And you say that to me!” cried Kolya. “And would you believe it, I thought—I’ve thought several times since I’ve been here—that you despised me! If only you knew how I value your opinion!”
“But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it, just now, when you were telling your story, I thought, as I watched you, that you must be very sensitive!”

“You thought so? What an eye you’ve got, I must say! I bet that was when I was talking about the goose. That was just when I was imagining you felt great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I quite hated you for it, and started talking like a fool. Then I imagined—just now, here—when I said that if there were no God He would have to be invented, that I was in too great a hurry to display my knowledge, especially since I got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn’t showing off out of vanity, though I really don’t know why. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I think it was because I was so pleased ... though it’s perfectly disgraceful for anyone to gush the moment they’re pleased, I know that. But I’m convinced now that you don’t despise me; it was all my imagination. Oh, Karamazov, I’m profoundly unhappy. I sometimes imagine all sorts of things, that everyone is laughing at me, the whole world, and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things.”
“And you worry everyone around you,” smiled Alyosha.
“Yes, I worry everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me, am I very ridiculous now?”

“Don’t think about that, don’t think of it at all!” cried Alyosha. “And what does ridiculous mean? Isn’t everyone constantly being or seeming ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people now are terribly afraid of being ridiculous, and that makes them unhappy. All I’m surprised at is that you should be feeling that so early, though I’ve noticed it for some time, and not only in you. Nowadays even children have begun to suffer from it. It’s almost a sort of insanity. The devil has taken the form of that vanity and entered the whole generation; it’s simply the devil,” added Alyosha, without a trace of the smile that Kolya, staring at him, expected to see. “You’re like everyone else,” said Alyosha, in conclusion, “that is, like very many others. Only you must not be like everybody else, that’s all.”
“Even if everyone is like that?”

“Yes, even if everyone is like that. You be the only one who isn’t. You really aren’t like everyone else: here you weren’t ashamed to confess to something bad and even ridiculous. And who will admit that much these days? No one. And people have even stopped feeling the urge to criticize themselves. Don’t be like everyone else, even if you’re the only one.”

“Splendid! I wasn’t mistaken in you. You know how to console a person. Oh, how I’ve longed to know you, Karamazov! I’ve been eager for this meeting for ages. Can you really have thought about me, too? You said just now that you thought of me, too?”
“Yes, I’d heard of you and had thought of you, too ... and if it’s partly vanity that makes you ask, it doesn’t matter.”
“Do you know, Karamazov, our talk has been like a declaration of love,” said Kolya, in a bashful and melting voice. “That’s not ridiculous, is it?”
“Not at all ridiculous, and if it were, it wouldn’t matter, because it’s been a good thing.” Alyosha smiled brightly.
“But do you know, Karamazov, you have to admit that you’re a little ashamed yourself, now.... I can see it in your eyes.” Kolya smiled with a sort of sly happiness.
“Why ashamed?”
“Well, why are you blushing?”
“It was you who made me blush,” laughed Alyosha, and he really did blush. “Oh, well, I am a little, goodness knows why, I don’t know...” he muttered, almost embarrassed.
“Oh, how I love you and admire you at this moment, just because you’re a little ashamed! Because you’re just like me,” cried Kolya, in sheer ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes beamed.
“You know, Kolya, you will be very unhappy in your life,” something made Alyosha say suddenly.
“I know, I know. How you know it all beforehand!” Kolya agreed at once.
“But you will bless life on the whole, all the same.”

“Just so, hurrah! You’re a prophet. Oh, we’ll get on together, Karamazov! Do you know, what delights me most is that you treat me quite like an equal. But we’re not equals, no, we’re not, you’re better! But we’ll get on. Do you know, all this last month I’ve been saying to myself, ‘Either we’ll be friends at once, forever, or we’ll part enemies to the grave!’”
“And saying that, of course, you loved me,” Alyosha laughed gaily.
“I did. I loved you awfully. I’ve been loving you and dreaming of you. And how do you know it all beforehand? Ah, here’s the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!”
